senses.d: The upper leg of a human, between the hip and the knee.
ex: About ten days ago, in cocking a pistol in the guard-room at Marcau, he accidentally shot himself through the Thigh.
‘Why not pay up now, kiddo?’ he suggested magnanimously, patting me on the thigh.

senses.d: That part of the leg of vertebrates (or sometimes other animals) which corresponds to the human thigh in position or function; the tibia of a horse, the tarsus of a bird; the third leg-section of an insect.
ex: Add the chicken thighs, close the bag, and squish the marinade to coat the chicken.
The newly discovered dinosaur Brontomerus mcintoshi may have used its huge muscular thighs to kick predators and rivals.

senses.d: A sensation of dryness in the throat associated with a craving for liquids, produced by deprivation of drink, or by some other cause (such as fear, excitement, etc.) which stops the secretion of the pharyngeal mucous membrane.
ex: We developed a great thirst during our hike.
He had quite a thirst on and so headed to his favourite Dublin pub.

senses.d: The condition producing the sensation of thirst.
ex: If you go out in the desert for long without water, the thirst can drive you mad.

senses.d: A want and eager desire (for something); a craving or longing.

ety.text: From Middle English thikkenesse, thiknesse, from Old English þicnes (“thickness, viscosity, density, hardness; obscurity, cloud, darkness; thicket; depth, a thick body, anything thick or heavy”), from Proto-West Germanic *þikkwīnassī (“thickness”), equivalent to thick + -ness. Cognate with West Frisian tsjokkens (“thickness”), Old High German dickinessī, dikkinissi, diknissi (“thickness, density”). Eclipsed non-native Middle English crassitude (“thickness”) from Latin crassitūdō (“thickness”).
